title: Remarkably Early Historical Information for the Resurrection of Jesus - Gary Habermas
summary: Habermas argues that early, critically-accepted data (homologia, pre-Pauline creeds, Paul's conversion, and Paul's Jerusalem consultations with Peter and James) establish eyewitness testimony to the resurrection within 2-6 years of the cross, defeating 'telephone tag' myth objections. He also distinguishes factual from emotional doubt and closes with exhortation from 1 Cor 15:58.

atoms.name: Resurrection is Christianity's load-bearing claim
atoms.statementTechnical: If Jesus was raised from the dead, Christianity is true; all other doctrinal disputes are non-fundamental.
atoms.statementPlain: If Jesus rose, Christianity is true; you don't have to solve every Bible problem.
atoms.falsificationCondition: Demonstration that Jesus did not rise (e.g., tomb not empty / body produced) would falsify Christianity on this axiom.

atoms.name: Homologia: earliest agreed-upon gospel data
atoms.statementTechnical: The earliest agreed-upon data (homologia) in the early church centered on Jesus' deity, death, and resurrection, preached immediately after the crucifixion.
atoms.statementPlain: The first Christians' earliest agreed message was the death and resurrection of Jesus, preached right away.
atoms.falsificationCondition: Evidence that earliest Christian preaching centered on other topics, or that resurrection preaching began decades later, would falsify.

atoms.name: Pre-Pauline creeds date within 1-2 years of the cross
atoms.statementTechnical: Early creedal formulations (memorizable summaries of the homologia) originated in Jerusalem within 1-2 years of the crucifixion, likely from the apostles, and Paul probably knew them all.
atoms.statementPlain: The earliest Christian creeds came from Jerusalem within a year or two of Jesus' death, from the apostles themselves.
atoms.falsificationCondition: Demonstration that the creeds postdate Paul or originate outside Jerusalem/apostolic circles would falsify.

atoms.name: Paul's conversion within 2-3 years of the cross
atoms.statementTechnical: Paul was converted approximately 2-3 years after the crucifixion, an event granted by critical scholars, giving an eyewitness link to the earliest data.
atoms.statementPlain: Paul became a Christian just two or three years after Jesus died.
atoms.falsificationCondition: Evidence that Paul's conversion occurred much later, or that he had no contact with pre-resurrection eyewitnesses, would falsify.

atoms.name: Paul verified the gospel with Peter and James (Gal 1-2)
atoms.statementTechnical: Paul visited Jerusalem ~3 years post-conversion (Gal 1:18) spending 15 days with Peter and James, and again 14 years later (Gal 2:2,9) where the pillars added nothing to his gospel and gave the right hand of fellowship.
atoms.statementPlain: Paul checked his gospel with Peter and James, the eyewitnesses, and they confirmed it.
atoms.falsificationCondition: Demonstration that Galatians is late/inauthentic, or that Paul's Jerusalem visits did not involve gospel verification with eyewitnesses, would falsify.

atoms.name: Early eyewitness chain rules out 'telephone tag' myth
atoms.statementTechnical: The 2-6 year chain from cross to Paul's verified contact with Peter and James precludes legendary development ('telephone tag'), since myths require far longer transmission.
atoms.statementPlain: The data is too early for the story to be a garbled myth.
atoms.falsificationCondition: A demonstrated case of a comparable myth forming within 2-6 years among multiple living eyewitnesses would falsify.
atoms.notes: Habermas rejects 'too early to be myth' as a slogan but defends the underlying chronology.

atoms.name: Gospels are Greco-Roman biographies
atoms.statementTechnical: Following a University of London doctoral dissertation, the majority critical view now classifies the Gospels as Greco-Roman bios, i.e., historiographical work.
atoms.statementPlain: Scholars now agree the Gospels are biographies, not a special Holy Spirit genre.
atoms.falsificationCondition: Scholarly consensus reverting to non-biographical genre classification would falsify.

atoms.name: Most doubt is emotional, not factual
atoms.statementTechnical: Clinical-psychological testing of Christians' doubts shows the great majority are emotional rather than factual, characterized by 'what if' questions and affective pain, and are not resolved by evidence.
atoms.statementPlain: Most doubt isn't about facts; it's emotional, and data won't fix it.
atoms.falsificationCondition: Psychological data showing most religious doubt is evidence-driven and resolved by evidence would falsify.
atoms.notes: Habermas cites co-work with a clinical psychologist.

atoms.name: 80% of early creedal material centers on death and resurrection
atoms.statementTechnical: Approximately 80% of the homologia and creedal material in the New Testament concerns Jesus' death and resurrection, indicating divine prioritization of the gospel core.
atoms.statementPlain: Most of the earliest Christian statements are about Jesus' death and resurrection.
atoms.falsificationCondition: Content analysis showing creedal material predominantly addresses other topics would falsify.

atoms.name: Post-salvation works determine eternal capacity for reward
atoms.statementTechnical: Good works do not save, but post-salvation labor in the Lord is not in vain and determines the capacity of eternal enjoyment (1 Cor 15:58).
atoms.statementPlain: Works don't save you, but what you do after salvation shapes your eternity.
atoms.falsificationCondition: Scriptural or theological demonstration that post-salvation works have no bearing on eternal reward would falsify.

atoms.name: Alexander the Great source gap (~300-450 yrs)
atoms.statementTechnical: Earliest source for Alexander is ~300 years after his death; best sources (Arrian, Plutarch) 425-450 years later.
atoms.statementPlain: We trust Alexander sources written centuries later but doubt Gospels written decades later.

atoms.name: Buddhist scriptures 600-800 years after Buddha
atoms.statementTechnical: A PhD Buddhist scholar concedes Buddhist sources date 600-800 years after Buddha's death, with no chain of Lord/disciple sources comparable to Christianity's.
atoms.statementPlain: Buddhist texts are far later than the Gospels.

atoms.name: Audience recall of 65-year-old events
atoms.statementTechnical: Audience poll shows many clearly recall eyewitness events from 65+ years prior, undercutting the claim that John's late date destroys reliability.
atoms.statementPlain: People really do remember things from 65 years ago.

atoms.name: Critical dating of NT documents
atoms.statementTechnical: Critical (including non-Christian) scholars date Mark ~70, Matthew ~80, Luke ~85, John ~90-95, 1 Thessalonians ~50, Paul's epistles 50-60.
atoms.statementPlain: Even skeptical scholars date the sources early.

atoms.name: Telephone-tag / myth objection
atoms.statementTechnical: If the gospel message were garbled transmission over decades, the resurrection data would be unreliable.

atoms.name: Jesus mythicism
atoms.statementTechnical: If Jesus never lived, all resurrection claims collapse.
atoms.notes: Habermas notes only two accredited scholars hold this; Ehrman wrote against it.

atoms.name: 'Christianity is too easy — just believe'
atoms.statementTechnical: Objection that salvation by belief alone is trivial; Habermas replies that NT 'believe' (pisteuo) means trust/surrender, like marriage vows.

atoms.name: 'If the data is so good, why don't critics believe?'
atoms.statementTechnical: Habermas answers that worldview commitments, not data, drive most disbelief.

atoms.name: Pharisaic historiographical method behind Paul's verification
atoms.statementTechnical: Josephus documents Pharisaic teaching-by-repetition and historical transmission; Paul, a Pharisee, applied this method in questioning Peter and James (historesai).
atoms.statementPlain: Paul checked the facts the way Pharisees were trained to.

atoms.name: Eight critical-accepted lines of evidence
atoms.statementTechnical: Eight separate lines of evidence from cross to end of Paul's epistles are accepted by critical scholars; four presented here.

atoms.name: God uses wounded lives
atoms.statementTechnical: Peter, James, and Paul each failed grievously yet were commissioned; application: God uses wounded lives.

atoms.name: Unclassified closing exhortation material
atoms.statementPlain: Exhortation on steadfastness, reward, and Christ's victory over death (1 Cor 15:55-58).
atoms.notes: Devotional close; not a discrete falsifiable claim.
